deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The bundle concerns the electrostatics of parallel circular cylinders ('ElektrCyl'), treated as a 2-D potential problem. The previous page has the following pieces. u(x,y) is harmonic, with u = p on one boundary curve and u = p_1 on the other. u is the real part of an analytic function u+vi. The conjugate v is obtained by v = ∫(u_x dy − u_y dx). v is in general multivalued with period k around the inner conductor. Cauchy's formula ∫(u+vi) dz/(z−z0) = 2πi(u0+v0 i) is evaluated with z−z0 = r e^{iφ}.

(1) MEAN VALUE. With dz/(z−z0) = i dφ on the circle, Cauchy's formula gives ∫_0^{2π}(u+vi) dφ = 2π(u0+v0 i). Taking real parts: u0 = (1/2π)∫_0^{2π} u dφ. This is the mean-value property of harmonic functions. On the previous page it is used to conclude that u has no interior maximum or minimum.

(2) NORMALIZATION TO AN ANNULUS (implicit step mine). If v increases by k on one circuit of the inner conductor, then w = (2π/k)(u+vi) increases by 2πi. Hence 𝔷 = exp((2π/k)(u+vi)) is single-valued. It maps the doubly connected region between the two conductors onto the annulus exp(2πp/k) < |𝔷| < exp(2πp_1/k), with the two boundary curves going to the two concentric circles. This explains the figure of two concentric circles. In the figure the outer curve is drawn doubled or wavy, perhaps suggesting a general outer boundary.

(3) 'Diese Function zu finden' — to find this mapping function, Riemann states a continuation principle. Suppose u = 0 on the line x = 0. Define the function at the mirror point −x+yi as −u+vi, where u+vi is its value at x+yi. Then this defines a continuous (indeed analytic) continuation, and in only one way ('und auf eine Weise stetig fortsetzbar'). In modern form: if f is analytic for x > 0 and Re f = 0 on x = 0, then g(z) = −conj(f(−conj z)) continues f analytically across the imaginary axis. This is the Schwarz reflection principle in the version 'real part vanishes on a line'.

(4) TRANSFER TO CIRCLES. The boundary circles in the z-plane are C: |z−a| = r and C_1: |z−a_1| = r_1. In the 𝔷-plane they are |𝔷| = ϱ and |𝔷| = ϱ_1. Riemann writes z' for the conjugate of z. On C, log(z−a) − log r has zero real part, so it plays the role of the variable x+yi in (3). The mirror point z* = a + r²/(z'−a') then corresponds to log r − log(z'−a'), which equals −conj(log((z−a)/r)): real part negated, imaginary part kept. Likewise in the image plane log 𝔷 − log ϱ corresponds to log ϱ − log 𝔷'. After exponentiating, the reflection pairs are (z−a)/r ↔ r/(z'−a') and 𝔷/ϱ ↔ ϱ/𝔷'. The same pairs hold with a_1, r_1, ϱ_1 (one cancelled attempt omitted a'_1).

The implied functional relation (mine, confirmed by the next page's ψ(r²/(z'−a')+a) = ϱ/ψ… and z = ψ(ζ)) is f(a + r²/(z'−a')) = ϱ²/conj f(z). Similarly f(a_1 + r_1²/(z'−a'_1)) = ϱ_1²/conj f(z). So the mapping function extends by repeated reflection in both circles. The composition of the two inversions in the 𝔷-plane is 𝔷 ↦ (ϱ_1/ϱ)² 𝔷. In the z-plane it is a hyperbolic Möbius map. This is the germ of the reflection-group (Schottky) method for mapping regions bounded by circles. It underlies Riemann's posthumous fragment on the equilibrium of electricity on cylinders with circular cross-section and parallel axes.
errors: No mathematical errors. The reflection formula −u+vi at −x+yi is correct for the condition u = 0 on x = 0.
The text says 'deren imaginärer Bestandtheil', but the condition actually used is x = 0, i.e. the variable is purely imaginary. This is either a slip or loose wording.
The circle formulas hold only modulo 2πi in the logarithms. This is harmless after exponentiation.
The uniqueness claim ('auf eine Weise') is asserted without justification. It is correct by the identity theorem.

results.what: Mean value of a harmonic function over a circle, derived from Cauchy's integral formula
results.modern_name: Mean value property / Gauss mean value theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1840) for potentials; Cauchy integral formula (1831)

results.what: Normalizing the multivalued complex potential by 2π/k and exponentiating to map the region between two conductors to an annulus
results.modern_name: Conformal map of a doubly connected domain onto an annulus via the complex potential (modulus/capacity)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (dissertation era) / later Schottky, Koebe for general theory

results.what: Continuation of an analytic function across a line on which its real part vanishes, by f(−x+yi) = −u+vi
Reflection in circles: (z−a)/r ↔ r/(z'−a') and 𝔷/ϱ ↔ ϱ/𝔷', giving f(a+r²/(z̄−ā)) = ϱ²/conj f(z) and continuation by repeated reflection in two circles
results.modern_name: Reflection principle for circles / symmetry principle; reflection (Schottky-type) groups
results.usually_credited_to: Schwarz (1870); Schottky (1877) for groups generated by reflections in circles

deep.surprise_reason: The mean value property and the annulus normalization are routine. The explicit reflection principle and its use for circles, with continuation by successive reflections in two circles, predates Schwarz's 1870 publication and Schottky's 1877 work. However, Riemann's use of symmetry/reflection is already known from his posthumously published lectures and from the Nachlass fragment on electricity on circular cylinders edited by Weber. This page looks like a working draft of that known material, so it is a notable but not unknown detail.

transcription_corrections: 'Folgendes {+Princip[?]+}': the inserted word is plausibly 'Princip', consistent with the reflection principle that follows.

'deren imaginärer Bestandtheil entgegengesetzt[?] gegeben' is uncertain. The mathematics concerns values at x+yi and −x+yi with u = 0 on x = 0; the reading 'entgegengesetzt gleich' or a similar phrase is possible.
'und auf eine Weise stetig fortsetzbar' may read 'nur auf eine Weise'; the first word is partly cancelled.
The symbol rendered '∓' between the paired fractions is better read as a correspondence mark (↔ / 'entspricht') than as plus-minus.
z' denotes the complex conjugate of z, so z'−a' = conj(z−a) and 𝔷' = conj(𝔷). This should be noted to avoid misreading z' as a second variable.
'r_1 a . r_1, a_1' should read 'r, a . r_1, a_1' (data of the first and second circle).
